title: Finding the right boundary via an insertion point
summary: In a sorted integer array, subtract 1 from the insertion point of target + 1 to obtain a candidate right-boundary index; before returning, confirm that the index is valid and its element equals target.
context: The sorted integer array is nums = [1, 3, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 10, 12, 15] and the target element is target = 6, with five consecutive 6s at indices 2 through 6. The figure shows the final two-pointer states for both the left-boundary search and the right-boundary search.
description: The left side directly executes “Find the leftmost target”: when the binary-search insertion-point search finishes, pointer i stops at index 2 (the first 6, cyan cell) and pointer j stops at index 1 (value 3), so the left boundary of 6 is i = 2.

The right side shows the two-way “Equivalent” reduction between “Find the rightmost target” and “Find the leftmost target + 1”: searching for the insertion point of target + 1 = 7 leaves pointer i at the first element greater than or equal to 7 (value 10 at index 7), while pointer j = i - 1 lands right on the last 6 at index 6 (cyan cell). Note that element 7 does not exist in the array; “Find the leftmost target + 1” in the figure means calling the insertion-point function to find the left-boundary insertion index i = 7 for 7, not matching an element 7.

frames.title: Finding the right boundary via an insertion point
frames.explanation: This equivalence relies on all array elements being integers: every element greater than 6 in the array is at least 7, so the first position holding a value of at least 7 is also the first position holding a value greater than 6. In actual code, after computing j = i - 1, you must still check that j is in bounds and nums[j] == target; otherwise target is absent from the array and -1 should be returned.
